prompt: The 21 replies of Vale Verde's order reach the aggregator mixed with replies to other orders. Which header field lets it sort them?
hint: What this message belongs to, not what it is.

choices.text: The correlation id, which names the order each reply belongs to
choices.why: Right: every part and every reply carries the chain's order number there, so the aggregator groups by it.

choices.text: The message id of each reply
choices.why: A message id identifies one message, and all 21 replies have different ones; it cannot say which belong together.

choices.text: The return address, the reply channel
choices.why: The return address says where a reply goes. Replies to many orders share that channel, so it cannot tell them apart.

choices.text: The timestamp, since the replies of one order arrive close together
choices.why: Replies of different orders interleave in time, and a slow branch can reply minutes after the rest.

prompt: Match each kind of message to the Serra Alta example the lesson gives for it.
hint: Do this, here is data, this happened.

pairs.right: create this store order in SAP
the monthly price table sent to the Portal B2B

right_distractors: the channel a reply should be sent to

prompt: A colleague's diagram shows a translator icon with one channel going in and three coming out. Reading it in the book's notation, what is wrong?
hint: Each icon promises a count of messages in and out.

choices.text: Nothing: a translator may send its output wherever it likes
choices.why: A translator changes a message and leaves its destination alone; choosing among exits is a router's job.

choices.text: The channels should be drawn as arrows
choices.why: How a channel is drawn is a matter of style; the count of exits is the substance.

choices.text: It promises one out: a router or splitter mislabelled
choices.why: Right: a translator is one in, one out. Three exits means the step also routes or splits, and the diagram hides it.

choices.text: A translator needs a return address
choices.why: A return address belongs to a request that expects a reply, not to a step in the middle of a flow.

prompt: Vale Verde's Tuesday order is for 9 stores. All 9 want milk from Juiz de Fora, 3 also want butter from Lavras and 6 want cheese from Alagoa. How many messages does the splitter produce?
hint: One message per store and plant.

prompt: Rui's aggregator completes only when the count of replies is reached. What happens on the morning one reply never comes?
hint: Nothing has failed yet, from its point of view.

choices.text: It sends a confirmation for the replies it has
choices.why: That is what a timeout would do. With a count alone it has no rule that lets it stop waiting.

choices.text: It raises an error, and the flow's alert fires
choices.why: No step has failed, so there is nothing to raise. That silence is why the defect lasted years.

choices.text: The broker redelivers the missing reply
choices.why: Redelivery applies to a message that exists. A reply that was never produced cannot be redelivered.

choices.text: It waits for ever, and the chain gets no confirmation
choices.why: Right: the aggregate stays open, nothing reports a failure, and the customer is the first to notice.

prompt: An aggregator times out at 06:12 and confirms the order without the cheese lines. At 06:25 the cheese reply arrives. If the aggregator kept no record of closed orders, what does it do?
hint: To the aggregator, a message with an unknown correlation id is a beginning.

choices.text: Starts a new aggregate and later sends a second confirmation
choices.why: Right: the late reply looks like the first of a new set. Remembering closed ids for longer than the timeout prevents it.

choices.text: Adds the cheese lines to the confirmation it already sent to the chain
choices.why: The confirmation has left; nothing can add to it. A correction is a new message somebody has to design.

choices.text: Discards it, since the order is already closed
choices.why: It cannot know the order is closed: that knowledge is exactly the record it did not keep.

choices.text: Sends it to the dead letter queue
choices.why: The reply is well formed and processes normally; nothing about it looks like a poison message.

prompt: Match each routing pattern to what goes in and what comes out.
hint: Count the messages on each side.

pairs.right: one message in, the same message out on one of several channels
one message in, the same message out or nothing
one message in, a copy out on each of several channels
several messages in out of order, the same messages out in order

right_distractors: one message in, its body changed to the receiver's format

prompt: Six systems all exchange orders with each other, point to point. How many translators are needed?
hint: One for each ordered pair: n(n − 1).

prompt: Orders flow from three senders (EDI, the Portal B2B, Salesforce) to two receivers (SAP, Business Central), point to point. A marketplace is added as a fourth sender. How many translators does point to point need after the addition?
hint: Not n(n − 1): only senders talk to receivers.

prompt: The order flow's enricher looks up each store's ship-to number in SAP. An order arrives on Sunday at 02:30. What happens?
hint: Lesson 1 gave SAP's weekly window.

choices.text: Nothing unusual: the queues decouple the flow from SAP
choices.why: The queues decouple the steps from each other, but the enricher's lookup is a synchronous call.

choices.text: It fails at the enricher, since SAP is down until 05:00, and orders queue behind it
choices.why: Right: the enricher hides a synchronous call, so the flow inherits SAP's Sunday maintenance window.

choices.text: The enricher skips the lookup and passes the order on
choices.why: An enricher that skipped silently would send SAP orders with no ship-to; nothing in the pattern does that.

choices.text: The EDI provider holds the order until Monday
choices.why: The provider delivered it already; the wait happens inside Serra Alta's flow.

prompt: Rather than send a 2 MB certificate through every hop, the message carries the Documentum object id, and the receiver fetches the PDF when it needs it. The book calls this a ___ check.
hint: Like the ticket for a coat left at a cloakroom.

prompt: Joana's company-wide canonical Customer reached 87 fields, nearly all optional. Why does a model like that fail as a contract?
hint: What can a receiver conclude from a record that validates?

choices.text: Because 87 fields make every message too large for MQ
choices.why: Field count is not the problem; a customer record is far below any message size limit.

choices.text: No receiver knows whether a record it gets is usable
choices.why: Right: with everything optional, a valid record promises nothing, and Customer means different things in each context.

choices.text: Because a canonical model never pays, whatever its scope
choices.why: Joana kept a canonical order message; scoped to one exchange with several parties, the model does pay.

choices.text: Because SAP's partner functions cannot be expressed in XML
choices.why: They can be written in any format; the trouble is that other systems mean something else by customer.

prompt: During the month close, Edson wants SAP to take store orders at no more than 50 a minute, whatever the queue holds. Which kind of consumer gives him that?
hint: Who decides when the next message is read?

choices.text: An event-driven consumer
choices.why: An event-driven consumer is handed messages as they arrive, so the queue sets the pace, not SAP.

choices.text: Three competing consumers
choices.why: Competing consumers raise throughput; Edson asked for a ceiling.

choices.text: A polling consumer
choices.why: Right: it asks for a message when it is ready, so asking 50 times a minute is the limit.

choices.text: A durable subscriber on a topic
choices.why: Durability keeps messages while a subscriber is away; it says nothing about how fast they are read.

prompt: The SAP branch reads a store order under syncpoint and calls the BAPI. SAP commits the sales order, then the flow fails before committing its get. What follows?
hint: Which of the two systems is in the unit of work?

choices.text: Both roll back, because the transaction also covers the BAPI call
choices.why: SAP's commit is not part of MQ's unit of work; nothing rolls the sales order back.

choices.text: It is redelivered, and without a check SAP gets a second order
choices.why: Right: the transaction protects the message, not the order, which is why the flow also checks for an existing order.

choices.text: The message is lost, since it was already read
choices.why: Under syncpoint an uncommitted get is undone, so the message goes back on the queue.

choices.text: MQ asks SAP whether the order exists before redelivering
choices.why: MQ knows nothing about SAP; that check is the receiver's job, which makes it an idempotent receiver.

prompt: Match each endpoint pattern to its Serra Alta example.
hint: Two of them hide messaging from code that does not want it.

pairs.right: Rota's code calls planPublisher.publish(plan) and never sees MQ
a queue's messages become calls to a BAPI that knows nothing about messages
three copies of the SAP order flow read the same queue
the Portal B2B gets the price changes published while it was redeployed

right_distractors: the store order is enriched with the ship-to number from SAP

prompt: Why did Rui talk Joana out of message selectors on one shared order queue, with Business Central taking Alagoa's orders and SAP the rest?
hint: Think of an order from a plant neither selector names.

choices.text: Selectors are not supported by IBM MQ
choices.why: MQ does support selectors; the objection is about what happens to messages they do not match.

choices.text: Business Central cannot read from MQ
choices.why: Business Central is reached through an adapter either way; the router design uses one too.

choices.text: Two consumers on one queue lose the order of messages
choices.why: That is the competing consumers trade-off; selectors split the messages by content rather than sharing them.

choices.text: Unmatched messages sit there unseen
choices.why: Right: an order from a new plant, or a typo, would wait on a queue that looks healthy. A router has a default exit.

prompt: What made the next farm-payment trace a search instead of a two-day project?
hint: The fix was not a new system.

choices.text: SAP's payment document number, carried to the bank and back
choices.why: Right: from the payment run to the return file the payment has one name, so a rejected line points at a vendor.

choices.text: A new mapping table from each hop's identifier to the next one's
choices.why: More tables are the problem, not the fix; the rule is to carry one identifier unchanged.

choices.text: Moving the payment run from the 10th to the 1st
choices.why: The date does not help anybody find a payment; the farms are paid on the 10th.

choices.text: Coleta sending SAP's vendor numbers
choices.why: Hops 1 and 2 were never the slow part; the trail went cold at the remittance.

prompt: Rui adds a wire tap and a message store to the remittance flow. Which of these does the lesson say must be decided with it? Choose all that apply.
hint: What is in the copies, and what if the copy fails?

choices.text: Who may read the store, since it holds farmers' bank accounts
choices.why: Yes: a copy of every message is a copy of the personal data in it.

choices.text: How long the copies are kept
choices.why: Yes: a retention period, decided before the store fills rather than after.

choices.text: What the main flow does if writing to the store fails
choices.why: Yes: the payment must still reach the bank, so the tap writes to a queue and something else fills the store.

choices.text: A new correlation id for each copy
choices.why: The opposite: a copy keeps the identifiers it had, or the store cannot be searched by them.

prompt: Serra Alta injects a synthetic order every morning at 05:00. What has to be true of every system downstream for this to be safe?
hint: What does a real sales order end in at Serra Alta?

choices.text: It answers within a minute
choices.why: Speed is what the test measures; safety is about the test not becoming a real order.

choices.text: It recognises the order as a test
choices.why: Right: a system that did not would treat it as real, and a real order ends in an NF-e the tax authority registers.

choices.text: It is switched to a test environment at 05:00
choices.why: Then the test would check the test environment; the point is to exercise production before the real orders arrive.

choices.text: Its queue is purged after the test
choices.why: Purging a production queue deletes whatever real messages are on it; that is the dangerous pattern.

prompt: Put the steps of the redesigned order flow in order, from the chain's order to its confirmation.
hint: After the review, enrichment happens on SAP's branch only.
items: Translate the EANCOM order into the bus's XML
Split it into one message per store and plant
Enrich the SAP-bound messages from the cache
Aggregate the replies by order number
Translate the result into an ORDRSP
trap: Enriching before the router is the defect the review found: it enriches messages for Business Central from SAP and stops them when SAP is down.

prompt: In the redesigned flow the enricher runs once per SAP-bound message, with no cache. An order of 50 lines splits into 26 messages, 5 of them for Alagoa. How many SAP lookups does it make?
hint: Alagoa's messages go to Business Central.

prompt: The router's default exit had carried three messages in two years. Why was Joana wrong to call it dead code?
hint: What were the three?

choices.text: Deleting a route needs a change window
choices.why: Windows decide when a change happens, not whether a route is needed.

choices.text: Rui's team uses it for test messages
choices.why: The test order goes through the normal route to SAP; the three were real orders.

choices.text: It is where unmatched orders wait to be seen
choices.why: Right: the three were real orders for a new product; without the exit they would have vanished.

choices.text: IIB refuses to deploy a Route node that has no default exit
choices.why: The argument is about the orders, not about the tool; a rule that only a tool enforces is not the reason.

prompt: Before a rep promises a delivery date, Talita wants Salesforce to ask both ERPs whether they can supply, and answer within ten seconds with whatever came back. Which composition fits?
hint: The same request to several receivers, and one answer.

choices.text: A splitter and a resequencer
choices.why: A splitter cuts one message into different parts; here both ERPs get the same question.

choices.text: A routing slip through SAP, then Business Central
choices.why: A slip visits the steps one after another, so the slowest ERP adds its whole time to the wait.

choices.text: A content-based router choosing one ERP per request
choices.why: A router sends each request to one destination; Talita wants both asked.

choices.text: Scatter-gather, with a timeout on the aggregator
choices.why: Right: a recipient list sends the same request to both, and the aggregator's timeout lets the answer come back in ten seconds.

prompt: A new design reads: "Portal B2B orders are enriched with credit data from SAP, split per delivery date, and aggregated into one confirmation." Which questions does the vocabulary tell a reviewer to ask? Choose all that apply.
hint: One question per pattern named.

choices.text: What does the enricher call, and what happens on Sunday from 01:00 to 05:00?
choices.why: Yes: an enricher hides a synchronous call, and SAP has a weekly window.

choices.text: Does each part carry the order number and how many parts there are?
choices.why: Yes: the aggregator correlates on the first and counts to the second.

choices.text: When is the aggregate complete if one part never comes back?
choices.why: Yes: count and timeout, and what the confirmation says about the missing part.

choices.text: Which ESQL nodes will implement each step?
choices.why: That is how it will be built, the description the vocabulary exists to get past.

prompt: The redesigned aggregator completes at 21 replies or after 30 minutes, whichever comes first. The second condition, the one that saves it from a lost reply, is its ___.
hint: A limit on waiting.

prompt: Farm onboarding sends a farm for a quality visit or a rejection letter depending on what its first milk sample showed. In the book's terms, what has to run it?
hint: Is the route known when the first message enters?

choices.text: A process manager, with state for each farm
choices.why: Right: the next step depends on an intermediate result, so the route needs state kept in one place.

choices.text: A routing slip attached when the request arrives
choices.why: A slip fixes the route at the start, and here the route is unknown until the sample is analysed.

choices.text: A message filter that drops failed farms
choices.why: A rejected farm still gets a letter; dropping the message would leave the farmer with no answer.

choices.text: A recipient list sending the farm to both the visit and the letter steps
choices.why: The two outcomes exclude each other; sending to both would visit a farm that was refused.
